entries.title: Serbia’s student-led movement nominates chemistry professor for presidency
entries.summary: Radomir Saicic, who teaches at Belgrade University, was among the first university professors to join the movement.
entries.content:
Radomir Saicic, who teaches at Belgrade University, was among the first university professors to join the student-led protest movement.

Serbia’s student-backed movement, which won an October election after rallying against corruption, has named university professor Radomir Saicic as its presidential candidate in next month’s polls.

Saicic, who teaches chemistry at Belgrade University, is a member of the newly elected parliament as a representative of the Student List, which won 140 seats in the 250-member parliament.

The role is largely ceremonial, but the president is responsible for nominating prime ministers and serves as commander-in-chief of the armed forces.

The December 27 presidential vote comes after Aleksandar Vucic – who dominated Serbian politics for 14 years – cut short his second presidential term to run for prime minister but was soundly defeated by the student-led movement in the parliamentary ballot.

Speaking at a televised news conference in Belgrade on Friday, Saicic said the movement must now prioritise strengthening the rule of law and fighting corruption.

“Now we have the opportunity to turn the freedom we fought for into lasting change,” he said.

“The assembly, the government and the courts must once again earn the trust of the people. The same applies to the institution of the president.”

Saicic pledged a “sovereign Serbia in which the constitution will be respected and in which every citizen will be able to live with dignity”.

Saicic, 65, is also a member of the Serbian Academy of Sciences and Arts, and was among the first university professors to join the student-led protest movement that emerged in 2024.

He said he was proud that students trusted him enough to put him forward as a presidential candidate, adding that “the last decade was marred by the crumbling of the rule of law, corruption and hate speech”.

“The outgoing regime is still trying to disintegrate our state,” he said. “In order to prevent this, we need to restore the institutions.”

Vucic, now an opposition member of parliament, has repeatedly suggested his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) might sit out the election, but a final decision is expected in mid-December.

Vucic himself is barred from running again as the constitution limits presidents to two terms.

The parliamentary and presidential elections followed nearly two years of protests sparked by the 2024 collapse of a railway station canopy in Novi Sad that killed 16 people.

The disaster at the recently renovated station, widely blamed on corruption, triggered Serbia’s largest protests since the fall of strongman Slobodan Milosevic in 2000.

The movement’s initial demand for a transparent investigation evolved into calls for snap elections, which Vucic eventually announced after nearly two years of resistance.

entries.title: Canada’s top court largely upholds Quebec’s religious symbols ban
entries.summary: Quebec’s ban on teachers and police wearing religious symbols such as hijabs and turbans on the job remains in place.
entries.content:
Quebec’s ban on teachers and police wearing religious symbols such as hijabs and turbans at work remains in place.

A landmark ruling by Canada’s Supreme Court has largely upheld Quebec’s secularism law, leaving in place a ban on public school teachers, police officers and some other public employees wearing religious symbols at work.

The ruling settles a years-long legal battle over a law that has forced some workers to choose between their careers and how they practice their faith.

The court left the ban in place, with one exception for elected members of Quebec’s National Assembly. The court found that require them to uncover their faces infringes upon their democratic rights.

The court also weighed in on a question that goes beyond Quebec — how far governments can go in using the notwithstanding clause.

The clause is part of Canada’s Charter of Rights and Freedoms. It lets federal and provincial governments keep a law in force even if it violates certain Charter rights, including freedom of religion and the right to equality, shielding it from court challenges. The override lasts up to five years and can be renewed. Quebec used it when it passed Bill 21 in 2019 and renewed it in 2024.

On Friday, the Supreme Court said politicians can use the clause without waiting for a court to rule on whether a law violates Charter rights. Four of the seven justices also agreed that judges can formally declare that a law violates those rights, as judges in lower courts had done, even if the clause keeps the law in effect.

What the law does

Quebec passed Bill 21 in June 2019, saying it would protect the religious neutrality of public institutions. It bars people in certain public jobs from wearing religious symbols such as hijabs, turbans and kippahs while at work. Teachers who were already in their posts on March 27, 2019, were able to continue wearing them as long as they stayed in the same role with the same employer.

The law has reshaped lives, leading to people losing their jobs and leaving Quebec to avoid the restrictions. Some Muslim women have decided to take off their hijabs while at work in order to be able to keep their jobs.

Quebec has since widened the restrictions to support staff and volunteers at school, as well as daycare workers.

What the judges said about the ban

The case was heard by seven justices. Chief Justice Richard Wagner, writing for three justices, said Bill 21 was rooted in Quebec’s “legitimate and historical commitment” to keeping the state secular. He concluded that the Quebec government had “validly used” its power to keep the law in force.

In a partial dissent, Justices Andromache Karakatsanis and Michelle O’Bonsawin wrote there was no question that the law violates the right to freedom of religion. They described how Muslim women had been turned away from jobs because they wear a hijab and how the law had prevented people from taking promotions or being transferred to new roles because they would lose their exemptions. They also said the law “non-trivially influences life choices and mobility”.

“The Act’s effects are not experienced equally,” they wrote. “They fall most heavily on Muslim women.”

How the case reached the court

Quebec invoked the notwithstanding clause when it passed Bill 21, before any court had ruled on the law. The override lasts up to five years and can be renewed. Quebec renewed it in 2024.

A Quebec Superior Court judge upheld most of the law in 2021, but found that it infringed certain rights that the clause cannot override, including the minority-language education rights of English-language school boards. Quebec’s Court of Appeal reversed the exemption for those boards in 2024 and left most of the law in place. Seven Supreme Court justices heard the case over four days in March.

entries.title: ‘Playing with fire’: Republicans incensed after Trump gets Huang reinstated
entries.summary: Former Trump officials warn his push to reinstate NVIDIA's CEO could be the final straw for Republicans.
entries.content:
Former Trump officials warn his push to reinstate NVIDIA’s CEO could be the final straw for Republicans.

United States President Donald Trump’s involvement in getting NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang reinstated has drawn little support from his own party with some Republican officials warning this could be a blow to the president’s popularity with his conservative base.

Earlier this week, the US president ignited a firestorm across Washington, DC, after he revealed he personally contacted NVIDIA’s board of directors and “convinced” its members to let Huang return.

Trump said he spoke to the board “directly and indirectly” in the less than two weeks between Huang’s resignation and his reinstatement, amid revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.

The move amounted to an extraordinary intervention by the US president, whose predecessors, both Democratic and Republican, have largely avoided personally involving themselves – or their administrations – in corporate matters.

“I felt very strongly about it,” Trump told CNBC on Monday about his decision to contact NVIDIA’s board. “And I felt more strongly as I saw what was happening with the … company, because that was, to me, a very important part of our country.”

After Huang’s resignation, shares of NVIDIA, which financial disclosures show Trump holds tens of millions of dollars of stock in, dropped sharply, wiping out more than $1tn in market value. They rebounded after Huang was reinstated.

A White House spokesperson told Al Jazeera that “Trump’s stock and bond portfolio is independently managed by third-party financial institutions” and neither Trump nor any of his family members has input on how investments are made.

Several Republican lawmakers in the US Senate have publicly objected to Huang’s reinstatement, expressing alarm that China, via the tech executive’s affair, may have obtained access to NVIDIA’s chips for its artificial intelligence arms race against the US. They have not, however, mentioned Trump’s foray into the matter.

“The controversy with Nvidia and Megaspeed is just the tip of the iceberg, and it’s not resolved because Jensen Huang has his job back,” Republican Senator Tom Cotton, a member of the Congressional-Executive Commission on China and the Chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee, posted to social media. “Congress has much to investigate and we will pass overwhelmingly bipartisan chip-export control bills, including my Chip Security Act, one way or the other.”

US Senate Majority Leader John Thune, who will continue to lead Republicans in the chamber when they enter the minority at the start of the next Congress in January, told Al Jazeera in a statement that Huang’s actions create “a significant national security vulnerability”.

“Through vigorous oversight and adoption of strong, bipartisan export-control measures, Congress will do its part to ensure our national security interests are being met,” Thune said. “The American people expect and deserve no less.”

Trump said NVIDIA’s board sought assurances that Huang did not pose a national security risk because of his relationship with Alice Huang, the former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed whom US officials suspect of working for China’s Ministry of State Security. Beijing has denied the allegation.

The US president, who said the NVIDIA CEO had been “exonerated”, noted that his assessment aligned with one conducted by the US Department of Justice. But in a news conference on Tuesday, US Attorney General Todd Blanche sidestepped questions about a reported investigation into Huang.

Privately, several former US Republican officials have told Al Jazeera it could be the final straw after a decade with a leader that some in the GOP have said has never been bound by traditional conservative principles.

“How very President Xi of him,” a former Trump administration official, speaking on condition of anonymity to speak candidly, said of the US president’s “communist-esque” actions in getting involved with NVIDIA, likening them to ones taken by the Chinese leader. “I think that sets a dangerous precedent.”

The official, who worked with Trump in the White House during his first term, described the modern-day US Republican Party as a tripod supported by three key values: religion, free market economics and national security.

But after Trump said he intervened with NVIDIA’s board to get Huang back on top, a leg of the “conservative stool,” they said, was broken.

“You need all three to stand. And he just ripped one out,” the official said. “So, at some point, the chair falls.”

“If he’s going to betray national security … why wouldn’t he betray the other legs, you know, on social conservative and economic issues?” they added. “I think it raises a lot of questions for folks and … he’s playing with fire.”

Ashley Davis, a Republican strategist who serves on several corporate boards, said NVIDIA, not Trump, will bear responsibility for reinstating Huang.

“If the president wants to make a phone call, because he’s concerned about chips or concerned about the macroeconomics of the impact of NVIDIA failing, that’s his prerogative,” Davis said. “It’s whether NVIDIA’s board wants to vote that way or not, and they did.”

Next week, Huang is slated to participate in a transcribed interview with the US House Foreign Affairs Committee, as well as a separate public hearing with the Senate Banking Committee.

One of the latter’s Republican members, Senator John Kennedy of Louisiana, said he expects Huang will “take the Fifth Amendment so he doesn’t incriminate himself in criminal prosecution.”

“It’s not my place as a senator to tell Mr Huang that he can’t cheat on his wife,” Kennedy told Fox News on Tuesday. “It is my place to tell him if you’re cheating on your wife with somebody who could be a Chinese spy, that jeopardises national security.”

A separate former Trump administration official who also spoke on condition of anonymity to speak openly about the situation told Al Jazeera the hearings would be “awful” for the US president – and they might even lead to significant political ramifications for him.

“If they are as bad as I think they will be, you could see Republicans talking about impeachment”, they said.

But some doubt this will be Trump’s undoing, noting that he has bounced back before from actions that crossed red lines for many Republicans.

“We’ve asked ourselves that same question for 10 years: ‘Is this what will cause Republicans to speak out against Trump?” Doug Heye, a former director of communications for the Republican National Committee, said. “Who knows at this point?”

entries.title: Funeral prayers held for 31 victims of Egypt tanker crash
entries.summary: Funeral prayers were held at Cairo’s Al-Azhar Mosque on Friday for 31 people killed when a car collided with a tanker
entries.content:
Funeral prayers held for 31 victims of Egypt tanker crash

NewsFeed

Funeral prayers held for 31 victims of Egypt tanker crash

Funeral prayers were held at Cairo’s Al-Azhar Mosque on Friday for 31 people killed when a car collided with a tanker, which exploded in a fireball. The crash which also left 26 people injured comes less than three weeks after a train collision killed seven people.

Published On 27 Nov 2026

entries.title: Manchester United trigger Bruno Fernandes contract extension to 2028
entries.summary: The captain had said that a long-term contract renewal was on hold, but Premier League club exercised one-year option.
entries.content:
The captain had said that a long-term contract renewal was on hold, but Premier League club exercised one-year option.

Manchester United are understood to have extended Bruno Fernandes’ existing contract by 12 months, ending speculation about a pre-contract agreement with an overseas club.

The Professional Football Association’s Player of the Year was in the final year of his existing contract, which would have allowed him to speak with clubs outside the Premier League from January 1 about a move next summer.

Fernandes had revealed that negotiations about a new contract had been put on hold, adding to speculation that he could seek a move away from a team that are currently in the league relegation zone.

United, however, are understood to have triggered a clause in the current deal to keep Fernandes at the Old Trafford club until the end of the 2027-2028 season.

Fernandes joined United in January 2020 from Sporting Lisbon, against whom he scored twice in the two sides’ midweek Champions League 2-2 draw.

The attacking midfielder quickly became the club’s most important player and last season performed a record number of assists in a Premier League season, helping secure the return to Europe’s elite competition for this campaign.

A team source said the move suited both parties and left the door open to future talks over a ⁠⁠new contract, although the immediate priority was improving results.

United are languishing in 19th place in the Premier League after their worst start to a top-flight season in 40 years.

Fernandes a doubt for Manchester United against Brentford

United entertain Brentford in the Premier League on Saturday, marking new manager Mauricio Pochettino’s first home game in charge of the club.

Fernandes, however, is a doubt for the match after missing training on Friday due to illness.

“We don’t know,” Pochettino said on Friday when asked if Fernandes will play. “He’s affected by a virus from Portugal. He finished the game a little bit with a problem and today he could not be part of the training session.”

“We’ll see during the day and [Saturday] how he wakes up. We’re not going to take any risks. When this type of situation happens, you don’t feel right. We are ⁠⁠going to pay attention, but still we have decided nothing.”

Pochettino is still searching for his first victory after the dramatic draw in Lisbon and a 4-0 ⁠⁠Premier League thrashing by Liverpool last weekend, although United were encouraged by their improved display in Portugal.

“We arrive full of energy, ⁠⁠positive, but it’s difficult for the players when the results ⁠⁠haven’t been up to scratch. We try to help them as best we can,” Pochettino said of his first week in charge.

“This is a group of players who want to do well, who want to perform. Our ‌‌job is to build confidence.”

On the speculation that had been swirling around Fernandes’ future in Manchester, following reports he had turned down two new contract offers, the Portugal midfielder said on Tuesday ‌‌that ‌‌talks could wait until results improve.

“I’m more worried about getting results, trying to bring the club back in a position to be proud of,” he said.

entries.title: Haaland ‘happy’ at Man City despite outburst that led to transfer talk
entries.summary: Erling Haaland blasted beleaguered City's form, but ahead of Arsenal test, manager Enzo Maresca says striker is happy.
entries.content:
Erling Haaland blasted beleaguered City’s form, but ahead of Arsenal test, manager Enzo Maresca says striker is happy.

Enzo Maresca insisted on Friday that Erling Haaland is “happy” at Manchester City after the striker expressed frustration over his side’s recent struggles.

Haaland gave a candid assessment of City’s malaise following Tuesday’s 2-2 draw against Napoli in the Champions League, which came on the back of a Premier League draw at home with Fulham.

After winning 10 of their first 11 matches in all competitions this season, Maresca’s men have won just two of their last seven.

With a crucial trip to Premier League leaders Arsenal looming on Sunday, Haaland’s criticism added to the growing sense that City’s season is in danger of spiralling out of control.

“We have to do better and find some ways to control the game more and perform in a better way,” Haaland said.

“I have no idea what we were missing but you could feel it in the last few games that something was not clicking fully.”

Haaland has scored just once in his last five games for City and is without a league goal in his past three matches.

The Norway star’s body language has been noticeably angst-ridden in recent weeks, prompting suggestions that he is growing disillusioned with life at the Etihad Stadium.

City are also awaiting the result of their appeal against a guilty verdict over breaches of Premier League financial rules, with the punishment potentially including a huge points deduction.

Despite City’s woes, Maresca is adamant Haaland remains committed to the cause regardless of speculation that he could seek a move at the end of the season.

“Erling is a nine; they live for goals and winning games. If they don’t score, they are upset. I think he gesticulates in the same way when we are winning games,” Maresca told reporters on Friday.

“For sure he is not happy because we are not winning games. But it is not just Erling. Everyone is on the same page.

“He has been good. He has been normal since day one. Two or three weeks ago, he was dancing inside the pitch and in the training sessions.

“He is happy. It is normal that results affect the mood a little bit but I don’t see any problem with Erling. He is a winner.”

Maresca will need Haaland back to his best against Arsenal if third-placed City are to earn a vital victory over the champions.

Already trailing six points behind Arsenal, a defeat in north London would be a huge blow to their title hopes.

Maresca has come under fire during City’s slump in his first season after replacing Pep Guardiola.

The former Chelsea boss claimed teething problems were inevitable during the transition from Guardiola’s dynastic reign.

“Transition requires time. It’s probably because we won seven games in a row, everyone was thinking at City there’s no transition,” Maresca said.

“But I’ve said many times I’m not a magician. There are eight or nine new players, the manager is new.

“For sure, when you don’t win games, it’s not the ideal situation. For me, it’s completely normal, I’m completely relaxed, no panic at all.”

entries.title: Why is Israel celebrating Costa Rica’s ban on Francesca Albanese?
entries.summary: Costa Rica is under pressure over its decision to bar the UN expert who has documented Israel's genocidal war on Gaza.
entries.content:
Costa Rica is under pressure over its decision to bar the UN expert who has documented Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.

Costa Rica has banned United Nations independent rapporteur Francesca Albanese from entering the country over what officials described as the risk she poses to national security.

Albanese has been one of Israel’s foremost critics, documenting its genocidal war on Gaza as well as its systematic discrimination against Palestinians and illegal settlement in occupied Palestinian territory since 1967.

Albanese was stopped by police on security grounds on Thursday as she arrived at Juan Santamaria international airport in the capital San Jose, where she was due to be presented with an honorary degree from the University of Costa Rica.

Albanese, who called the move “a disgrace”, was still being held at the airport on Friday.

Omer Badilla, the director-general of Costa Rica’s immigration authority, later appeared to offer some explanation on social media, saying Albanese “was refused entry to the country because she is the subject of an international alert due to links to terrorist acts”, without specifying the nature of that alert or which country had issued it.

“It is important to note that when national security is at risk, as is the case here,” Badilla continued without elaborating. “Our police authorities strictly enforce the provisions of our legal system.”

While the move was welcomed by Israel, including by its Ambassador to the UN, Danny Danon, a number of Costa Rican and regional figures and rights groups, as well as the University of Costa Rica, have objected to the treatment of Albanese and demanded an explanation.

On Thursday, the Association of Human Rights Lawyers, Judges and Prosecutors of Latin America and the Caribbean (AJUFIDH) urged the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights to seek answers from the Costa Rican government, arguing that the ban may violate international obligations protecting UN experts.

Costa Rican lawmakers from several political parties have also criticised the move, describing it as arbitrary and damaging to the country’s reputation for defending human rights and international law, while the university has formally requested that immigration authorities and foreign ministry officials explain the legal grounds for the decision.

Why would Israel celebrate a UN figure not being allowed entry to Costa Rica?

As Special Rapporteur, Albanese has used her position to document Israeli violations of international law. She accuses Israel of committing genocide in Gaza, maintaining an apartheid system against Palestinians and pursuing territorial expansion through illegal settlements in occupied East Jerusalem and the West Bank.

In her March 2024 report, Anatomy of a Genocide, for which she received numerous threats, Albanese found that there were reasonable grounds to conclude that Israel had committed acts prohibited under the UN Genocide Convention. She subsequently called for an arms embargo, sanctions against Israel and an end to the trade and financial relationships sustaining its occupation.

Throughout her tenure, Albanese has repeatedly described the occupation of Palestinian territory as an entrenched system of apartheid and settler colonialism, arguing that the displacement of Palestinians and expansion of illegal Israeli settlements are part of a much wider process of territorial dispossession.

She has also challenged Israel’s international backers, accusing governments of providing diplomatic protection and military assistance while failing to uphold their obligations under international law.

In her July 2025 report, she went further still, naming companies including Microsoft, Amazon and Google, alongside arms manufacturers and financial institutions, which she said were helping to sustain Israel’s occupation and military campaign. She called on governments to sever trade and financial ties with Israel, impose an arms embargo and hold companies accountable.

On Friday, Balkees Jarrah, Middle East and North Africa director at Human Rights Watch, told Al Jazeera: “The Costa Rican authorities’ decision to bar Francesca Albanese entry comes in the context of increasing efforts aimed at muzzling criticism of Israeli authorities’ atrocity crimes against Palestinians, ensuring impunity for these abuses, and other governments’ complicity in them.”

Who is Francesca Albanese?

Born to a lawyer and a homemaker in a small town in the Campania region of southern Italy in 1977, Albanese has said her interest in Israeli-Palestinian politics was shaped by her father’s library, where she encountered the writings of Holocaust survivor Primo Levi. She was also inspired by her older brother’s bedroom posters supporting Palestine during the first Intifada.

After studying law at the University of Pisa and human rights at SOAS in London, she pursued a career with the UN, first in Africa, then in Geneva and finally in Jerusalem with UNRWA, the UN agency for Palestinian refugees, before going on to be appointed Special Rapporteur on human rights in the occupied Palestinian territories in May 2022.

Is this the first time Israel and its allies have targeted Albanese?

No.

Israel and its supporters have been campaigning against Albanese for years, repeatedly accusing her of anti-Semitism and anti-Israel bias and calling for her removal from her UN post.

The campaign intensified in 2023, when Israel and pro-Israel organisations stepped up demands for her dismissal following allegations that some of her public comments crossed the line into anti-Semitism.

In January that year, 11 US members of Congress signed a bipartisan letter urging the UN to remove her, while Israeli government officials also called for her resignation. Albanese rejected the accusations, saying they were intended to discredit her work documenting Israeli abuses.

The most significant escalation came in July 2025, when the Trump administration imposed sanctions against Albanese, accusing her of pursuing a campaign of political and economic warfare against Israel and the United States.

The measures included restrictions on Albanese entering the US, blocking her property and financial interests subject to US jurisdiction and prohibiting US nationals from engaging in transactions with her, effectively isolating her from much of the US financial system.

The US decision was roundly condemned by the UN and various rights groups.

A committee of the UN’s Human Rights Council characterised it as just one aspect of the “continued assault of the current US administration on the entire UN system and its core values of human rights, justice, accountability and the rule of law”. Rights groups, including Human Rights Watch (HRW) and Amnesty International, also criticised the decision, with the latter slamming the US measures as a “disgraceful affront to international justice”.

entries.title: Why did Georgian police clash with Turkish football fans over Palestine?
entries.summary: Georgia's Interior Ministry says 16 people were detained and three employees injured during clashes.
entries.content:
Georgia’s Interior Ministry says 16 people were detained and three ministry employees injured during clashes.

Police in Georgia have detained at least 16 people following clashes between football fans at a game between Turkish and Israeli clubs.

The Europa League fifth round match between Turkiye’s Besiktas and Israel’s Hapoel Be’er Sheva was hosted in Georgia instead of Turkiye.

The coastal Georgian city of Batumi was selected last month as a neutral territory to host the game for “safety and security reasons” because of fears of protests over Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, according to the European football association, UEFA.

Despite the precaution, tensions between fans spilled over into the stadium and the match was suspended for 30 minutes. Once play resumed, Besiktas won the game 2-1.

It is not the first time violent clashes have marred football matches involving Israeli clubs since Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza began in October 2023.

Here’s what we know about the latest unrest:

What happened in Besiktas and Hapoel Be’er Sheva’s game?

Tensions between fans had already been rising before kickoff in Batumi on Thursday.

According to the Georgian news outlet Civil Georgia, videos on social media showed groups of Besiktas fans marching through Batumi and physical confrontations between fans and police officers.

Turkiye’s Anadolu Agency reported that the Besiktas players refused to shake hands with their Hapoel opposition.

In the 26th minute, the game was temporarily suspended when clashes broke out between Georgian police and Besiktas supporters. Turkish media outlets reported that police entered the stands and used pepper spray against Turkish fans.

According to reports, the police involvement came after a fan displayed a Palestinian flag and banner.

Turkiye’s TRT World reported that police surrounded the fan and used pepper spray, adding that video later showed a Besiktas fan being carried out on a stretcher and others being injured during the intervention.

What have Turkiye and Georgia said after Europa League match?

Omer Celik, spokesperson and deputy chairman of Turkiye’s ruling AK party, posted on X that the “intervention and violence” against the Besiktas fans who unfurled a ‘FREEDOM FOR PALESTINE’ banner and held a Palestine flag was “unacceptable”.

“Besiktas fans spoke on behalf of the alliance of humanity and became the voice of humanity. We strongly condemn the Israeli team’s provocations on the pitch. We extend our best wishes for a speedy recovery to our fans who were injured in the incidents and taken to hospital. We are closely monitoring the condition of our citizens,” Celik said.

But Georgian Interior Minister Sulkhan Tamazashvili told reporters that UEFA officials confiscated the fans’ Palestine flags and Georgian state authorities played no role in the confiscation.

Tamazashvili said that 16 people were detained and three ministry employees injured.

“While marching from European Square towards Batumi Arena, some of the fans of the football club ‘Besiktas’ stood out by their aggressive actions,” the ministry said in a statement.

“They violated the public order by making indecent shouting and shooting of various objects, disobeyed the legal demands of the police, resisted law enforcement and physically confronted them.”

Police took appropriate measures to curb the violence, de-escalate incidents and ensure public safety, including the use of what it called “special means”, the ministry added.

It denied that the use of force was related to the display of pro-Palestine banners and flags.

“We categorically deny this information and emphasise that violent actions by fans and physical confrontation with law enforcers prior to the display of flags and banners have just begun while marching towards the stadium.”

How have Besiktas and other Turkish clubs responded?

Besiktas said it condemned the use of “disproportionate force”.

“We have initiated formal inquiries with our Consulate General in Batumi and with UEFA regarding the disproportionate force used by security personnel against our supporters; we will continue to monitor the situation closely until every single one of our supporters has returned home safely,” read a club statement.

In a post on X congratulating the Besiktas victory, the Turkish Football Federation said it would “closely monitor the unacceptable behaviour directed at our club, Besiktas and our supporters in Batumi tonight, and that we will take action with the relevant authorities to ensure that these incidents are fully investigated and the necessary steps are taken.”

Other Turkish Super Lig clubs, including Trabzonspor, Fenerbahce, Galatasaray, Erzurumspor, Basaksehir and Samsunspor, also condemned the use of force against Besiktas fans.

Why was Georgia hosting a UEFA match between Israeli and Turkish teams?

Since the onset of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza three years ago, Turkish clubs have not hosted Israeli opposition at home because of security concerns, with matches played in neutral territories instead.

Turkish-Israeli relations have taken a downturn since the war began, with Turkish authorities taking a hard line against the military policies of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government in the occupied Palestinian territories.

However, Georgia and Israel have good relations with close ties maintained amid the war.

Israel’s far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir was in the capital Tbilisi for a diplomatic visit last year.

What’s Europe’s track record when dealing with pro-Palestine fans?

Not great.

Last year, English club Aston Villa hosted a Europa League game against Maccabi Tel Aviv, but security concerns prompted West Midlands Police to recommend the banning of Israeli fans from the game.

The decision was taken following violence after a match in Amsterdam between Maccabi and Dutch side Ajax. Police intervened against protesters and Israeli media framed the clashes as a “violent, anti-Semitic pogrom”.

In 2024, another match between Ajax and Maccabi Tel Aviv led to clashes between fans of the Israeli team and pro-Palestine protesters, as Maccabi fans burned Palestinian flags and attacked homes displaying them.

entries.title: Eisenkot navigates tricky waters as he tests power-sharing with Netanyahu
entries.summary: Some of his allies are calling for such an arrangement, but it would represent a betrayal of his pre-election promise.
entries.content:
Some of his allies are calling for such an arrangement, but it would represent a betrayal of his pre-election promise.

The 2026 Israeli elections were termed the most consequential in recent decades for the country – for multiple reasons.

For Benjamin Netanyahu, the caretaker prime minister, and his right-wing coalition, the elections were about keeping the far-right in power to protect the formative changes they enacted in state policies and institutions. For the anti-Netanyahu bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot – or the “change bloc”, as it is referred to – the promise was to replace the failed October 7 government as they termed it, rehabilitate Israel’s international standing, and end internal divisions.

Once the results were announced, things changed. Gadi Eisenkot was tasked with forming Israel’s next government. But his bloc does not have enough seats in the Knesset to win a vote of confidence on its own. The United Arab List and the Joint List, parties led by Palestinian citizens of Israel, have 19 seats and are willing to back Eisenkot in his efforts to replace Netanyahu as Israel’s premier. But some in the change bloc, such as Avigdor Lieberman, promised not to support any government coalition that includes an Arab-led party or one that depended on votes from Palestinian citizens of Israel.

This, despite the fact that Lieberman himself became chair of the Knesset’s Foreign Affairs and Defense Committee thanks to those same votes. That contradiction was pointed out by Mohamed Majadli, the chief editor of AlNas Radio in Israel and an analyst on the country’s Channel 12.

In such a limited space for political manoeuvres, Eisenkot embarked on forming a coalition, holding talks with his partners, while also trying to open channels of communication with ultra-Orthodox parties, particularly the United Torah Judaism party. At the same time, former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett led efforts to form a unity government with Netanyahu’s Likud party and succeeded in convincing Eisenkot’s Yashar party to open formal talks with Likud.

The prospect of reneging on the change bloc’s central promise to oust Netanyahu looms large over these talks. Bennett and others are advocating for that outcome in light of the lack of a clear Zionist majority against Israel’s longest-serving prime minister.

Meanwhile, leader of the Democrats group, Yair Golan, has publicly opposed any unity formula with Netanyahu and has called out Bennett for his efforts to reach it. The Yashar-Likud talks are complex and overshadowed by, among other issues, accusations between the two sides.

Netanyahu accuses the change bloc of working to undermine Israel by working with Arab-led parties, which he has referred to as “the enemy”. Eisenkot has gone on the record saying that Netanyahu endangers the security of Israel and is willing to ignite war for his personal gain.

From Likud’s perspective, a unity government would require a rotation agreement on the premiership. That means that rather than getting rid of Netanyahu, Eisenkot would have to agree to Netanyahu staying on as prime minister for two years, or agreeing to serve second in the rotation.

This scenario gained traction after judges presiding over Netanyahu corruption trials recommended dropping the most serious charge of bribery, as well as reconsidering the charges or reaching a plea bargain in the others. This development has strengthened Netanyahu’s negotiating position and prompted him to call for an end to the political boycott against him.

Against this backdrop, Eisenkot is manoeuvring through dangerous political waters. If he fails to form a government, voters may be forced to return to the polls again while Netanyahu remains at the helm. This scenario could translate into a loss of support for the change bloc and hand Netanyahu a renewed mandate, while simultaneously ending the political careers of some leaders such as Eisenkot.

If Eisenkot chooses unity with Netanyahu over the promises he made to his voters, he will lose credibility among supporters. Additionally, Eisenkot could be outmanoeuvred by Netanyahu.

Many point to the coalition agreement between Benjamin Netanyahu and Benny Gantz in 2020, which included a rotating premiership. The government collapsed before Benny Gantz assumed his position and his political career never recovered.

In political terms, forming a unity government with Netanyahu would represent a reversal of election promises on fundamental issues such as transparency, judicial reform, and the influence of religion on the state, because unlike the change bloc, Netanyahu’s allies are already embedded in the state bureaucracy and able to entrench these policies.

More strategically, it reflects the knee-jerk reaction of Israel’s body politic to Palestinian citizens of Israel. This is what leading sociologist and researcher Honaida Ghanem calls Israel’s structural problem: its inability to reconcile that part of Israel’s political and leadership crisis is that in today’s Israel, anti-Arab sentiment is one of the few policies most Jewish Israelis can agree on, while they no longer agree on the nature of the state, the influence of religion over the state, or many other fundamental issues of identity and governance.

The prospect of a unity government with Eisenkot and Netanyahu remains possible, though not likely, primarily because of the personal and political risks such an unholy political marriage would entail for the change bloc leaders.

entries.title: Famine expect to rise due to global conflict, El Nino, warns UN
entries.summary: El Nino is a major driver behind three of the four newly identified hotspots, mainly in different parts of Africa.
entries.content:
El Nino is a major driver behind three of the four newly identified hotspots, mainly in different parts of Africa.

Hunger ‌is set to worsen significantly in 16 global hotspots over the coming six ⁠months, mainly due to armed conflict and extreme climate events, two United Nations agencies said in a new report.

The Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) and World Food Programme (WFP) warned on Friday that Sudan, South Sudan, Somalia, northern Nigeria and Yemen ⁠faced the gravest threats of famine, driven by violence, displacement, economic hardship and extreme weather, including the El Nino phenomenon.

Listings in the report, released twice a year through the Global Network Against Food Crises, have risen from 13 hotspots in June, with ⁠Chad, Uganda and parts of both Southern Africa and Central America added, while Lebanon was removed.

Armed conflict and violence were driving hunger in 12 of the 16 hotspots, the report said, as soaring food, energy ⁠and transport costs were eroding people’s ability to feed themselves.

El Nino, which is set to intensify to exceptional levels in the coming months according to the World Meteorological Organization (WMO), is a major driver behind three of the four newly identified hotspots: Southern Africa, the Central American Dry Corridor and northeastern Uganda.

Covering December 2026 to May 2027, the agencies warned that shrinking humanitarian funding was affecting efforts to avert catastrophe.

In the five countries most at risk, all repeatedly cited on the hotspot list since 2022, humanitarian assistance has declined by nearly two-thirds over the 2022-2025 period, from $5.1bn to $2bn.

“While conflict, economic shocks, climate extremes and access constraints have remained the primary drivers of these crises, declining humanitarian resources have reduced the capacity to sustain gains and mitigate worsening conditions,” wrote the FAO and WFP.

While past humanitarian assistance helped avert famine, “the gains proved fragile and of limited duration: severe acute food insecurity risks – including risk of famine – re-emerged within a few years.”

In Sudan, famine remains a risk ⁠in 13 areas of North Darfur and South Kordofan through January 2027, as fighting disrupts food production, markets and aid deliveries.

The agencies also identified famine risks in parts of Somalia and South ‌Sudan, where escalating violence has compounded an already desperate humanitarian situation.

Afghanistan, Haiti, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Gaza were also classified as areas of very great concern.

Gaza was ‌downgraded ‌from the highest level of concern after small improvements in food security following the October 2025 “ceasefire”. But agencies warned that conditions remained fragile in Gaza, while in the occupied West Bank, acute food insecurity is expected to worsen.
